summary: Describes how to use Elliptic Curve Cryptography public key algorithms in the Cryptographic Message Syntax, for creating digital signatures and exchanging keys that protect content. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Elliptic curve math makes strong locks with small keys. This document explains how to use that math to sign and protect messages in a widely used format.

subtitle: How to sign and encrypt CMS messages with elliptic curve algorithms: ECDSA signatures plus ECDH and ECMQV key agreement.

tldr.problem: The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) is independent of any particular algorithm, so using elliptic curve public key algorithms in it needs a precise profile that says which fields, algorithms and encodings to use.
tldr.mechanism: ECDSA signs content in SignedData. Ephemeral-static ECDH and 1-Pass ECMQV derive a pairwise key-encryption key that wraps the content-encryption key (or the authentication key) for each recipient in EnvelopedData, AuthenticatedData and AuthEnvelopedData.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3278, adds SHA-2 hash options and AuthEnvelopedData, and sets a mandatory-to-implement baseline built around SHA-256 and AES-128.

facts.label: Mandatory EnvelopedData suite
facts.value: ECDH standard, SHA-256 KDF, AES-128 wrap, AES-128 CBC

today: RFC 5753 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 3278. The metadata for this site lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the ECC Profile Covers
sections.content:
CMS is algorithm independent. RFC 5753 is a profile that says how to plug Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) public key algorithms into four CMS content types:

  • SignedData uses ECDSA to sign content.
  • EnvelopedData uses ECDH or ECMQV key agreement to generate a pairwise key-encryption key that encrypts the content-encryption key.
  • AuthenticatedData uses ECMQV to generate a key-encryption key that protects the message-authentication key.
  • AuthEnvelopedData uses ECMQV to protect both an authentication key and an encryption key.

It also covers how EC public keys are distributed in certificates. The algorithm processing builds on NIST FIPS 186-3 for signatures, NIST SP800-56A and SEC1 for key agreement, and FIPS 180-3 for hashing. The document obsoletes RFC 3278.
sections.plainLanguage: CMS is a standard envelope for secret and signed mail. This document says how to use a special kind of small, strong lock in that envelope.

sections.title: Signing with ECDSA
sections.content:
In SignedData, ECDSA is used with the SHA family. The digestAlgorithm must be one of id-sha1, id-sha224, id-sha256, id-sha384 or id-sha512. The signatureAlgorithm is the matching ecdsa-with-SHA* identifier, and the hash named in it must be the same as the digest algorithm.

The signature field holds the DER encoding of an ECDSA-Sig-Value, a sequence of two integers, r and s. The sender uses the digest and signing steps of CMS with the FIPS 186-3 method, and the receiver retrieves r and s to verify. The certificates field may carry the certificates for the signing EC keys.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature is like a stamp only you can make. The signer stamps a short fingerprint of the message and anyone with your public key can check the stamp.

sections.title: Key Agreement for Encrypted Content
sections.content:
Instead of encrypting directly to a recipient, the sender and recipient agree on a shared secret and use it as a key-encryption key (KEK) to wrap the content-encryption key (CEK). Because key agreement is used, the CMS kari choice of RecipientInfo applies and KeyAgreeRecipientInfo version must be 3.

Ephemeral-static ECDH comes in two variants: standard ECDH (from SEC1) and co-factor ECDH (method C(1, 1, ECC CDH) from SP800-56A). The sender puts a fresh ephemeral EC public key in the originator field and uses the recipient's static key from its certificate. Static-static ECDH is not specified, because the ephemeral contribution gives better security. The optional ukm should be included, so a different KEK is generated even if an ephemeral key is wrongly reused.

1-Pass ECMQV (method C(1, 2, ECC MQV)) uses three key pairs: an ephemeral pair, the sender's static pair and the recipient's static pair. Here the ukm must be present and holds an MQVuserKeyingMaterial with the sender's ephemeral key. Because the sender's static key is involved, ECMQV can work with EnvelopedData, AuthenticatedData and AuthEnvelopedData, while ECDH works only in EnvelopedData.

Both methods run the key derivation function from Section 3.6.1 of SEC1, with the hash named by the key agreement algorithm, over an ECC-CMS-SharedInfo structure that contains the key-wrap algorithm, optional user keying material and the KEK length in bits. Public keys are encoded as ECPoint; implementations must support uncompressed points, may support compressed ones, and must not support hybrid ones.
sections.plainLanguage: Two people each mix a secret number with the other's public number and end up with the same secret, without ever sending it. They use that secret to lock the key that locks the message.

sections.title: Authenticated Data and Authenticated Encryption
sections.content:
AuthenticatedData lacks non-repudiation, so it can be preferable to SignedData, for example when the sender does not want the message to stay authenticated if it is forwarded. AuthEnvelopedData provides authentication and encryption together and can be preferable to signing and then encrypting. Both use 1-Pass ECMQV, and their KeyAgreeRecipientInfo fields and sender and receiver actions are the same as for EnvelopedData with 1-Pass ECMQV.

For AuthenticatedData the MAC algorithm must be one of HMAC with SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512. A caution applies to both types: data origin authentication with ECMQV is only reliable when there is exactly one recipient. With several, one recipient could modify the content without the others noticing, so a worried sender should use a separate message for each recipient.
sections.plainLanguage: If you send the same sealed note to many people, one of them could swap the note and tell the rest it came from you. So for that kind of proof, send each person their own copy.

sections.title: Required and Recommended Algorithms
sections.content:
Implementations are recommended to support SignedData and EnvelopedData; AuthenticatedData and AuthEnvelopedData are optional. Implementations should use the elliptic curve domain parameters specified by the PKIX document cited as [PKI-ALG].

  • ECDSA: must support ECDSA with SHA-256. For interoperability the P-192, P-224 and P-256 curves are recommended with SHA-256, P-384 with SHA-384, and P-521 with SHA-512.
  • EnvelopedData: if supported, ephemeral-static ECDH standard must be supported, while co-factor ECDH and 1-Pass ECMQV are optional. The must-support set is the SHA-256 key derivation scheme, id-aes128-wrap for key wrap and id-aes128-cbc for content encryption.
  • AuthenticatedData and AuthEnvelopedData: the mandatory set uses the ECMQV SHA-256 scheme with AES-128 key wrap, plus id-hmacWithSHA256 or id-aes128-ccm respectively.

Content encryption options include 3-key Triple DES, AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256 in CBC mode for EnvelopedData, and AES in CCM or GCM mode for AuthEnvelopedData.
sections.plainLanguage: To make sure everyone's tools fit together, the document names one basic set of locks every program must have and lets them add fancier ones if they like.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC warns that cryptographic algorithms are broken or weakened over time, so implementers and users should keep checking that the listed algorithms still give the expected security. They also rely on good random numbers.

Secret keys must be the right size: for elliptic curve groups the secret key size must equal the size of the group order n. Larger secret keys add no security and smaller ones are likely to reduce it dramatically. An attacker could also send oversized keys or certificates to swamp the processor, so agents that use such keys before validating the certificate to a trust anchor should have cryptographic resource management.

The RFC includes tables that map ECDH, ECMQV and ECDSA key sizes to minimum bits of security, with matching hash, key wrap, content encryption algorithms and named curves. It recommends keeping those choices roughly equivalent in strength, for example 128 bits of security with a 256-bit key, SHA-256, AES-128 and curve secp256r1. Users of MQV are also pointed to a known vulnerability described in a cited reference.
sections.plainLanguage: A chain is only as strong as its weakest link, so the lock, the key and the box should all be about equally strong.
